results.title: Where to Rent an H100 PCIe at the Cheapest Price (Oct 2026)
results.author: GPUBank Research
highlights:
The posted prices for an H100 PCIe hour ran from $0.81 to $3.50 at managed and marketplace providers when we checked on 15 and 16 October 2026, and the spread is mostly about what the hour buys rather than the silicon. Some prices cover the GPU alone, some include a full machine with disk, an IP address and traffic, some can be taken back with a few minutes of notice, and some require a three-year commitment. Stock was thin: Runpod, Lambda, GPU.ai and Oblivus were all shown out of stock, and Vast.ai's own page listed no offers on 16 October 8 7 6.

### The rest of the market

Beyond the six providers above, the rest of the market is a long tail of smaller clouds whose prices we could read only through trackers. ComputePrices showed QuantaCloud at $2.59 in the US Midwest, Omega Gradient at $2.63 in Canada, OVHcloud at $2.99 for its h100-380 flavour, which pairs the card with 30 vCPU, 380 GB of RAM and 3.84 TB of passthrough NVMe and reports itself to nvidia-smi as 'NVIDIA H100 PCIe' in Spare Cores' test 12, and AtmosCompute at $3.01, with Thunder Compute at $3.20 in an older reading dated 5 September, and GetDeploying showed Scaleway's single-card H100-1-80G at $3.21 in stock in Paris and Warsaw, Oblivus at $3.50 out of stock and Enverge at $4.00 8 13 7. Scaleway's own page confirms that both its flavours carry the PCIe card, with 24 vCPU and 240 GB of RAM on the single-GPU one, but did not show a price when we read it 14. io.net's own price guide, dated April 2026, gives $1.49 for an H100 PCIe on its decentralised network, a snapshot we could not refresh 15.

The marketplace readings move by the hour, so their history says more than any single number. GridCompute, which tracks Vast.ai hourly, counted four on-demand H100 PCIe listings with eight GPUs between them on 8 October, with a lowest ask of $1.25 and a median of $2.78, and the median had ranged from $1.63 to $3.52 since tracking began on 2 October 16. On the interruptible side GetDeploying showed a two-card Vast.ai listing in South Africa at $0.67 per GPU on 15 October, and Beam's own H100 article puts Vast.ai's interruptible offers 'around $0.35 per GPU-hour' 5 17. Lium, whose price includes the node's local disk, was tracked at $1.40 in Almaty on 29 September and at $2.15 in Boardman in the United States, with 26 vCPU and 221 GB of RAM, on 7 October 18. None of these hours comes with a fixed machine or a credit when the host goes away, and on Vast.ai the disk and bandwidth are billed on top of the ask 11.

Massed Compute sells an 'H100 (80GB)' at $2.73 an hour with 20 vCPU, 128 GB of RAM and 1,250 GB of storage, next to separate rows for the H100 NVL and the H100 SXM5, so by elimination it is the PCIe card even though the page never says so 19. On the marketplace side, Lium had no H100 PCIe free when we looked, only SXM listings, and OpenRelay was tracked at $2.20 20 8. None of these is a reason to skip the providers above, but QuantaCloud and Massed Compute are worth a look if you need a US machine with a large local disk and the cheaper clouds are sold out.

On 15 and 16 October 2026 an H100 PCIe cost between $1.35 and $3.50 an hour on demand at managed clouds, about $2.00 on marketplaces with stock and from $0.81 on interruptible capacity. GPUBank's own survey of public on-demand prices put the market average at $2.71 on 29 September 41. A full 730-hour month therefore runs from $985.50 to about $2,400 before storage, and the large clouds do not sell this card at all.

...

## What changes the price

The version. On-demand, the PCIe 80 GB starts at $1.99, the NVL 94 GB starts at $2.59 and the SXM 80 GB starts at $2.69. PCIe is a card that fits a standard server slot. It runs at lower power than SXM and links to other GPUs more slowly, and it is usually the cheaper version to rent. NVL is a PCIe card made to be paired with a second one over an NVLink bridge, so the two share data quickly. It draws less power than the SXM version. SXM is a module mounted on NVIDIA's HGX board, where GPUs share data over NVLink. It runs at full power with the fastest links between GPUs, which is why 8-GPU training machines use it.

The pricing type. The cheapest spot price, $1.29 at Azure, is 35% below the cheapest on-demand price. Spot capacity can be taken back at short notice; see spot or on-demand.

The provider. Each provider's cheapest on-demand price runs from $1.99 at RunPod to $6.98 at Azure: 3.5 times as much for the same GPU family.

results.title: Learnings from tracking GPU and token prices for fun - DEV Community
results.author: Paul Piper
highlights:
Learnings from tracking GPU and token prices for fun - DEV Community
Paul Piper
Posted on Oct 20 • Originally published at madppiper.substack.com
# Learnings from tracking GPU and token prices for fun
Part of my job, and honestly part of my hobby, is watching prices. Not all of them, of course (I mean, what a lunatic must you be), but specific ones: GPU and inference endpoints. A while back I noticed that they differ immensely across providers, so I built a tool. Smart Inference, the router Jenni and I run, reads the price of GPU rentals and LLM tokens from a list of providers around the clock and sends each request to the cheapest healthy option. Since April it has kept every price it ever saw, which by now is roughly 11 million GPU price points and 3.3 million token prices.
I was wondering if my own data would support my theory that there is “overcapacity in the market”. Alas, that is not really what it shows.
I start in June, because before that we had too few providers to say much. From June to October, the median hourly price of the GPUs everybody wants went up:
* H100, on-demand: 3.25 to 3.89 dollars (+20%)
* H200, on-demand: 4.00 to 5.02 dollars (+25%)
* B200, on-demand: 6.11 to 7.42 dollars (+21%)
* B200, spot: 2.14 to 3.78 dollars (+77%)
Meanwhile, even the spot pricing options jumped: H100 in June was offered at a low of 1.04 an hour, and was bumped to 1.81 in October. This fits the overall market trend.
There is one exception, however and that is older hardware: An A100 on spot went from 1.07 to 0.88 an hour back in July and has sat there ever since. So it looks like people are fighting over newer hardware and perhaps if you want to really make a bargain right now, those can be a better choice.
Then I looked at the token side (my inference endpoints) and that’s where it got weird: Across all providers that serve the same model, the median price per million input tokens shifted a lot. DeepSeek V4 was at 1.30 dollars until July and is selling for 0.30 now, about 77% less. GLM-5 went from 1.00 in May to 0.15 in October. Output tokens fell almost as hard (DeepSeek V4: 2.60 down to 1.20, GLM-5: 3.20 to 0.50).
So a steep price drop, even though the models are unchanged and hardware got more expensive. To be fair, not everything got cheaper. Kimi K2.6 and GLM-4.7 stayed roughly the same, and gpt-oss-120b even went up a little at the median. But the big new open models, the ones people actually switch to, lost three quarters of their price or more within a few months of launch.
All in all, hardware got about 20% more expensive and inference got 80% cheaper. Makes no sense, but okay…
I have some theories why that may be: sometimes models are subsidized, other times providers get better at running the models (quantization is a thing) and maybe, just maybe older models are downgraded to lower specs (which could also have an impact on performance).
Theories aside, what it shows, however, is that my own idea that “the market is producing vast overcapacity for AI” is not really the case. At least not according to the data. If that were the case, my own pricing table, which also features “spot pricing”, should get cheaper over time, not more expensive. For current hardware it looks more like the opposite, the GPUs get pricier. It also means that sometimes model providers are eating the costs.
That matters more than you may think: it means that at least for now, it is more expensive to run your own GPU than it is to build on inference infrastructure. If token prices drop faster than GPU prices, renting your own GPU stops making sense for most workloads, and buying tokens from whoever is cheapest this week wins. Six months ago I would have told you that self-hosting on spot GPUs was the smart move for steady traffic. Today, for the big open models, I would check the token price first.
Before I finish this, you should be aware that this observation is only based on our own data: every monthly median comes from two to seven providers, the mix changes from month to month as we onboard additional ones. So even though the data points are complete, we are only comparing a small subset of providers.
Anyway, I love to be proven wrong, so I will keep checking up on the market in the near future. I will keep you posted…

results.title: What It Actually Costs to Rent an H100, H200, or B200 in October 2026
results.author: Dex Mareno
highlights:
- As of late October 2026, the cheapest reliable on-demand H100 (80GB) is back around $1.99/GPU-hr (Voltage Park), with brand-name specialty clouds at ~$2.50 (Hyperstack PCIe), ~$2.89 (RunPod), and ~$2.90 SXM (Ori); the median 'cheapest' across two dozen providers is ~$3.33, and spot dips to ~$0.94 (Prime Intellect).
